title: Benign Conditions of the Penis and Scrotum
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains the common nonmalignant disorders of the penis and scrotum: erectile dysfunction, the fluid, blood, cystic, and venous swellings of the scrotum, testicular torsion, priapism, Peyronie disease, and the causes of male infertility. Each is taught from the normal anatomy and physiology that it disrupts, such as the veno-occlusive mechanism of erection, the embryology of the processus vaginalis, and the venous drainage of the testes. Board questions rely on a small set of bedside clues (transillumination, position relative to the testis, change with posture, the cremasteric reflex, nocturnal erections) and on hormone patterns, and each clue makes sense once its mechanism is clear.
prerequisites: Gross anatomy of the penis, scrotum, testis, epididymis, and spermatic cord (RE-2, RE-4)
Descent of the testis and the processus vaginalis (RE-1)
Autonomic and somatic innervation and venous drainage of the pelvis and genitalia (RE-5)
Hypothalamic, pituitary, and testicular hormones and their feedback (RE-7)
Nitric oxide, cGMP, and smooth muscle relaxation

connections.how: Atherosclerosis narrows the small penile arteries early, so vascular erectile dysfunction is often a sign of systemic arterial disease.
Renal cell carcinoma that grows into the left renal vein blocks drainage of the left testicular vein and produces a new left varicocele.
Sickled red cells obstruct outflow from the cavernous sinusoids and are a leading cause of ischemic priapism, especially in children and young men.
Cryptorchidism and Klinefelter syndrome are testicular causes of infertility, and CFTR mutations cause absence of the vas deferens.
Diabetes causes erectile dysfunction through neuropathy, endothelial dysfunction, and atherosclerosis at once, and it can cause retrograde ejaculation.

Involuntary erections that occur mainly during REM sleep and show that the nerves, vessels, and smooth muscle of erection are working.
The closed serous sac, derived from the processus vaginalis, that covers the front and sides of the testis.
A pouch of peritoneum that extends through the inguinal canal into the scrotum ahead of the descending testis.
Passage of light through a scrotal swelling; clear fluid transmits light, while blood, veins, and solid tissue do not.
The network of veins in the spermatic cord that surrounds the testicular artery and drains into the testicular vein.
A high attachment of the tunica vaginalis on the spermatic cord that leaves the testis free to rotate inside the sac.
Elevation of the testis by contraction of the cremaster muscle when the skin of the upper medial thigh is stroked (spinal segments L1 and L2).
A persistent, painful, rigid erection caused by failed venous outflow, with hypoxic and acidotic blood trapped in the corpora cavernosa.
The dense fibrous coat around each corpus cavernosum (and, separately, around the testis).
Complete absence of sperm in the ejaculate.
Gonadal failure caused by too little GnRH, LH, and FSH, so both the gonadotropins and testosterone are low.

sections.title: Erectile dysfunction: mechanism of erection and classification of causes

blocks.text: Erection is a neurovascular event. Sexual stimulation activates parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4 (the pelvic splanchnic nerves), which reach the penis in the cavernous nerves. Their nitrergic endings and the sinusoidal endothelium release nitric oxide (NO). NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase in smooth muscle, cyclic GMP (cGMP) activates protein kinase G, cytosolic Ca2+ falls, and the helicine arteries and trabecular smooth muscle relax. Inflow fills the sinusoids, which expand against the tunica albuginea and compress the subtunical venules. This veno-occlusive mechanism, not inflow alone, makes the penis rigid.

blocks.title: From stimulation to rigid erection
steps: Parasympathetic S2 to S4 fibers fire in the cavernous nerves
Nerve endings and endothelium release nitric oxide
Guanylyl cyclase raises cGMP; cytosolic Ca2+ falls
Helicine arteries and trabecular smooth muscle relax
Arterial inflow fills the cavernous sinusoids
Sinusoids compress subtunical venules: blood is trapped
blocks.caption: Failure at any step causes erectile dysfunction. Detumescence follows when PDE5 degrades cGMP and sympathetic alpha-1 tone contracts the smooth muscle.

blocks.text: Detumescence reverses the chain: phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) hydrolyzes cGMP, and sympathetic fibers from T11 to L2 release norepinephrine onto alpha-1 receptors, contracting smooth muscle so the sinusoids empty. Erectile dysfunction (ED) is the persistent inability to achieve or keep an erection adequate for intercourse, and its causes map onto the links of this chain.

blocks.title: Causes of erectile dysfunction by mechanism
rows: Narrowed penile arteries limit inflow; endothelial damage lowers NO; injured sinusoids leak (veno-occlusive failure)
Atherosclerosis, smoking, hypertension, aortoiliac occlusion (Leriche syndrome)
Gradual onset in all settings; other vascular disease
Parasympathetic outflow or cavernous nerves interrupted
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy, spinal cord injury, radical prostatectomy or other pelvic surgery, multiple sclerosis
Low testosterone lowers libido and NO-dependent signaling; prolactin suppresses GnRH pulses
Low libido, small testes, galactorrhea or headache
Thiazides, some beta blockers, SSRIs, antiandrogens, dopamine antagonists, opioids, alcohol
Central inhibition and high sympathetic tone override intact peripheral mechanisms
Sudden, situational onset; nocturnal erections preserved
blocks.caption: Organic causes often coexist; psychogenic ED is identified by intact nocturnal and morning erections.

blocks.text: Causes often combine. Diabetes damages autonomic nerves, impairs endothelial NO production through hyperglycemia and oxidative stress, and accelerates atherosclerosis. Because the penile arteries are narrow, plaque limits flow there early, so vascular ED often precedes symptomatic coronary disease by a few years and is regarded as a marker of systemic atherosclerosis.

Healthy men have about three to five erections a night, mostly during REM sleep, generated by brainstem mechanisms free of emotional inhibition. Preserved nocturnal or morning erections therefore show that nerves, vessels, smooth muscle, and androgen support all work, and the cause is psychogenic. Their absence points to an organic cause; low testosterone also reduces them.

Two pathways start erection. Psychogenic erection depends on descending input from the brain through thoracolumbar and sacral outflow. Reflexogenic erection uses a sacral arc: pudendal sensory fibers from the genitalia synapse in S2 to S4, which send parasympathetic output back to the penis.

blocks.predict: A man with a complete spinal cord transection at T6 is touched on the penis. Can he have an erection?
blocks.explain: Usually yes. The sacral reflex arc (pudendal afferents, S2 to S4 parasympathetic outflow) lies below the lesion and is intact, so reflexogenic erection persists. Psychogenic erection, which needs descending input from the brain, is lost.
blocks.check: The two pathways of erection and the neurogenic row of the table.

sections.title: Hematocele: blood in the tunica vaginalis

blocks.text: The tunica vaginalis is a closed serous sac. Its visceral layer covers the front and sides of the testis, its parietal layer lines the inner scrotal wall, and a thin film of fluid between them lets the testis move. A hematocele is blood collected in this space.

Blunt scrotal trauma is the most common cause, and it may rupture the tunica albuginea of the testis (testicular rupture), spilling blood and seminiferous tubules into the sac. Other causes are hemorrhagic infarction in torsion, bleeding from a testicular tumor, scrotal or inguinal surgery, and bleeding disorders or anticoagulation. Because a hematocele can conceal a ruptured, twisted, or neoplastic testis, the clinical question is always what lies beneath it.

Transillumination explains the key bedside test. A light held against the scrotum in a dark room scatters through clear serous fluid, so a hydrocele glows red. Hemoglobin absorbs visible light and clot is opaque, so a hematocele stays dark, as do solid tumors and veins. A hematocele is usually tense and tender, with overlying bruising, and the testis cannot be felt through it.

Over weeks an untreated hematocele organizes. Fibrin and granulation tissue thicken the sac wall, the clot fibroses, and the wall may calcify. A chronic hematocele can therefore present as a firm, painless mass that mimics a testicular tumor. A large, tense collection can also compress the testis. On ultrasound a hematocele is a complex collection with internal echoes and septations, whereas a simple hydrocele is anechoic (black).

blocks.title: Hydrocele compared with hematocele
rows: Infancy (patent processus) or idiopathic in adults; infection, trauma, tumor
Trauma, torsion, tumor, surgery, bleeding tendency
Often acute and painful, with bruising
Complex fluid with echoes and septations
Organizes, fibroses, may calcify and mimic tumor
blocks.caption: Both collections lie in the same space; their contents decide whether light passes through.

blocks.text: A hydrocele is serous fluid in the tunica vaginalis, and its two types follow from embryology. Before the testis descends, a pouch of peritoneum, the processus vaginalis, extends through the inguinal canal into the scrotal swelling, led by the gubernaculum. The testis descends behind this pouch and normally reaches the scrotum by about birth. The upper processus then closes, at or shortly after birth, and only the distal sac around the testis remains as the tunica vaginalis.

blocks.title: Fate of the processus vaginalis
rows: Upper part closed, distal sac left around testis
Indirect inguinal hernia (bowel or omentum can enter)
Closed above and below an isolated segment
Closed, fluid trapped or produced within the sac
blocks.caption: The same patent processus causes a communicating hydrocele or an indirect hernia, depending on the size of its opening.

blocks.text: In a communicating hydrocele, peritoneal fluid moves in and out through the patent processus. The swelling is smaller in the morning after lying flat and larger after activity, crying, or straining, and it may be reducible. It is common in infants, especially those born preterm, and shares its cause with indirect inguinal hernia.

A noncommunicating hydrocele has no connection with the peritoneum. Fluid accumulates because the mesothelium of the tunica vaginalis secretes more than its lymphatics reabsorb. In newborns, fluid trapped when the processus closed is usually absorbed during the first year. In adults most cases are idiopathic, but secondary hydroceles follow epididymitis or orchitis (more secretion), trauma, a testicular tumor (reactive fluid), and lymphatic obstruction, including filariasis from Wuchereria bancrofti and surgery that interrupts scrotal lymphatics.

On examination a hydrocele is a smooth, painless, fluctuant swelling that surrounds the testis, so the testis is hard to feel separately. It transilluminates. With a noncommunicating hydrocele the examiner can usually feel a normal cord above the swelling, which separates it from an inguinoscrotal hernia. Because fluid can hide a tumor, a new hydrocele in a young man calls for ultrasound of the testis. In infants, a hernia containing gas-filled bowel can also transilluminate, so light alone does not exclude a hernia.

blocks.predict: A 6-month-old has a scrotal swelling that is small each morning and large by evening. What anatomical defect explains the change?
blocks.explain: A patent processus vaginalis. Lying flat overnight lets fluid drain back into the peritoneal cavity; upright posture and crying push it down again. A noncommunicating hydrocele has no channel and does not change size this way.
blocks.check: The table on the fate of the processus vaginalis.

blocks.text: Sperm leave the seminiferous tubules through the rete testis, pass through about 12 to 20 efferent ductules into the head of the epididymis, and then travel through the single coiled duct of the epididymis to the vas deferens. A spermatocele is a retention cyst that forms when part of this outflow, usually an efferent ductule or the rete testis near the epididymal head, becomes obstructed and dilates. Because it is still connected to sperm-producing tubules, it fills with milky or opalescent fluid containing spermatozoa. Its lining is flattened or cuboidal epithelium.

A spermatocele is a smooth, painless, fluctuant mass, usually at the head of the epididymis above and behind the testis. Because it arises from the epididymis rather than filling the space around the testis, the testis can be felt separately below it. This separation is the main bedside distinction from a hydrocele, which surrounds the testis. A spermatocele transilluminates, although its cloudier fluid may glow less brightly than a hydrocele.

A simple epididymal cyst is a fluid-filled cyst of the epididymis that contains clear fluid without sperm. It can occur anywhere along the epididymis and is often multiple. Clinically and on ultrasound it looks the same as a spermatocele: both are smooth, transilluminating, and separate from the testis. They are told apart only by the contents, sperm or no sperm, if the fluid is aspirated or examined after excision. Both are benign, have no malignant potential, and are common incidental findings in adults.

blocks.title: Cystic scrotal swellings that transilluminate
rows: Dilated efferent ductule or rete testis
Head of epididymis, above and behind testis
blocks.caption: Position relative to the testis separates epididymal swellings from a hydrocele; only the contents separate a spermatocele from an epididymal cyst.

sections.title: Varicocele: venous anatomy, infertility, and renal cell carcinoma

blocks.text: The testicular artery runs down the spermatic cord surrounded by the pampiniform plexus, a network of about 8 to 12 veins that join near the deep inguinal ring to form the testicular vein. Cool venous blood returning from the scrotum absorbs heat from the arterial blood beside it. This countercurrent heat exchange, with the thin scrotal skin and the cremaster and dartos muscles, keeps the testis at about 34 to 35 °C (93 to 95 °F), a few degrees below core temperature of 37 °C (98.6 °F). Spermatogenesis depends on that lower temperature.

A varicocele is dilation and tortuosity of the pampiniform plexus caused by reflux of blood down the testicular vein, usually through absent or incompetent valves. It appears around puberty and is found in about 15% of adult men and a much larger share of men evaluated for infertility. About 90% are left-sided. The left testicular vein is longer, enters the left renal vein at a right angle, and drains into a vein that can be compressed between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta, so its hydrostatic pressure is higher. The right testicular vein enters the inferior vena cava (IVC) directly at an oblique angle.

With the patient standing, a varicocele feels like a bag of worms above and behind the testis. It enlarges with standing or the Valsalva maneuver and collapses when he lies down, because gravity and abdominal pressure drive the reflux. It does not transilluminate, because it contains blood. It may cause a dull ache after prolonged standing, and the testis on that side may be smaller.

blocks.title: How a varicocele impairs spermatogenesis
steps: Incompetent valves allow reflux down the testicular vein
Pampiniform plexus dilates and warm blood pools
Countercurrent cooling of the testicular artery fails
Testicular temperature, oxidative stress, and hypoxia rise
Germ cell apoptosis and impaired Sertoli and Leydig function
Lower sperm count, motility, and normal morphology
blocks.caption: Raised temperature is the main mechanism; reflux of renal and adrenal venous metabolites may add to the injury on the left.

blocks.text: Not every varicocele causes infertility, but it is a common finding in infertile men, and a unilateral lesion can affect both testes through venous connections across the midline.

A varicocele can also be the first sign of obstruction higher up. Renal cell carcinoma characteristically grows into the renal vein. A tumor thrombus in the left renal vein blocks drainage of the left testicular vein and produces a new left varicocele, typically in an older man, that may not collapse when he lies down. A right-sided varicocele by itself, or one that persists when supine, suggests compression of the IVC or a retroperitoneal mass.

blocks.predict: A 58-year-old man has a new right-sided varicocele that stays the same size when he lies flat. Why is this more worrying than a left varicocele in a 17-year-old?
blocks.explain: The right testicular vein drains obliquely into the IVC, so valve failure alone rarely causes a right varicocele, and one that does not empty when supine is held open by obstruction, such as an IVC thrombus or retroperitoneal mass.
blocks.check: The left and right venous drainage and the paragraph on secondary varicocele.

blocks.title: Sorting four scrotal swellings at the bedside
blocks.text: Ask three questions. Does light pass through? Hydrocele and spermatocele transilluminate; hematocele and varicocele do not. Can the testis be felt separately? A hydrocele hides it, while a spermatocele sits above and behind it. What changes it? A varicocele fills on standing and empties lying down, a communicating hydrocele grows by day and shrinks overnight, and a hematocele follows trauma and is tender. A dark, tender mass after a kick needs the testis checked for rupture; a new left bag of worms in an older man needs the left kidney imaged.

Normally the tunica vaginalis covers only the front and sides of the testis, and the back of the testis and epididymis is anchored to the scrotal wall. In the bell-clapper deformity the tunica attaches high on the spermatic cord, so the testis hangs free inside the sac like the clapper of a bell and can rotate. The deformity is often present on both sides, so the opposite testis is also at risk. Rotation of the testis inside the tunica is intravaginal torsion, the type seen in adolescents, with a peak around puberty. Neonatal torsion is usually extravaginal: the whole cord and tunica twist above the testis before the tunica has fixed to the scrotum.

blocks.title: Torsion to infarction
steps: Bell-clapper deformity lets the testis rotate
Spermatic cord twists
Thin-walled, low-pressure veins collapse first
Arterial inflow continues: congestion, edema, hemorrhage
Pressure inside the inelastic tunica albuginea rises
Arterial inflow stops: hemorrhagic infarction
blocks.caption: Venous occlusion before arterial occlusion explains why the infarct is hemorrhagic rather than pale.

blocks.text: Viability depends on the duration of ischemia. Most testes survive if blood flow returns within about 6 hours, and few survive after about 24 hours, so torsion is a surgical emergency.

The classic presentation is sudden, severe, unilateral scrotal pain, often waking the patient or following exercise. Nausea and vomiting are common, and pain may be felt in the lower abdomen because visceral afferents from the testis follow the testicular vessels to lower thoracic segments around T10, where the testis originated. The twisted cord is shortened, so the testis rides high and may lie horizontally. The cremasteric reflex is normally elicited by stroking the upper medial thigh, with sensory fibers in the ilioinguinal nerve and femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve and motor fibers in the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1 and L2). In torsion it is usually absent; the testis is already drawn up on a twisted, edematous cord. Doppler ultrasound shows reduced or absent flow and sometimes a whirlpool pattern in the cord.

blocks.title: Acute scrotal pain: three common causes
rows: Sexually active men and older men
Tender nodule at upper pole; blue dot sign
blocks.caption: An absent cremasteric reflex and a high-riding testis favor torsion; inflammation increases rather than reduces blood flow.

blocks.text: Priapism is a full or partial erection lasting more than 4 hours that persists without, or beyond, sexual stimulation. It reflects failure of detumescence, which normally depends on cGMP breakdown and sympathetic alpha-1 contraction of cavernosal smooth muscle to reopen the venous outflow. There are two types with opposite physiology.

Ischemic (low-flow, veno-occlusive) priapism accounts for most cases. Venous outflow from the corpora cavernosa fails, inflow then stops, and the trapped blood becomes hypoxic, hypercapnic, and acidotic, like blood in a closed compartment. The corpora cavernosa are rigid and painful, while the glans and corpus spongiosum usually stay soft. Cavernosal blood is dark, with pO2 below about 30 mmHg, pCO2 above about 60 mmHg, and pH below about 7.25.

Sickle cell disease is the most common cause in children. Slow, relatively deoxygenated sinusoidal blood promotes polymerization of hemoglobin S, and rigid sickled cells obstruct outflow; disordered NO and PDE5 signaling also contributes, and many patients have recurrent brief (stuttering) episodes. Drug causes include agents injected into the corpora to relax smooth muscle, drugs with alpha-1 blocking activity such as prazosin, trazodone, and some antipsychotics (which remove the sympathetic contraction needed for detumescence), and cocaine. Leukemia with hyperviscosity is another cause.

blocks.title: The self-sustaining cycle of ischemic priapism
steps: Venous outflow from the sinusoids is blocked
Trapped blood becomes hypoxic and acidotic
Hypoxic smooth muscle cannot contract
Sinusoids stay dilated and keep compressing the venules
Outflow remains blocked
blocks.caption: Hypoxia and acidosis prevent the smooth muscle contraction that would end the erection, so the cycle persists until it is broken.

blocks.text: Prolonged ischemia injures the cavernosal tissue progressively: edema of the trabeculae within about 12 hours, loss of sinusoidal endothelium and platelet adherence by about 24 hours, and thrombosis with smooth muscle necrosis by about 48 hours. Necrotic smooth muscle is replaced by fibrous tissue, which cannot relax or compress the venules, so persistent ischemic priapism ends in permanent erectile dysfunction from veno-occlusive failure.

blocks.title: Ischemic compared with nonischemic priapism
rows: Unregulated arterial inflow through a cavernosal artery to sinusoid fistula
Dark; low pO2, high pCO2, acidotic
Bright red; similar to arterial blood
blocks.caption: Blood gas analysis of cavernosal blood separates the two types.

blocks.text: Each corpus cavernosum is wrapped in the tunica albuginea, a layer of dense collagen with elastic fibers that must stretch evenly for the erect penis to stay straight. Peyronie disease is a localized fibrous plaque in the tunica albuginea. Robbins groups it with the superficial fibromatoses, together with palmar fibromatosis (Dupuytren contracture), and the two conditions are associated. It mainly affects men aged about 40 to 70.

The favored mechanism is repeated microtrauma to the tunica during intercourse in a predisposed man. Bleeding and fibrin deposition in the tunica trigger inflammation, transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) activates fibroblasts to become myofibroblasts, and disorganized collagen is laid down instead of normal elastic tissue. Risk is higher with age, diabetes, and Dupuytren contracture. Histologically the plaque is dense, poorly cellular collagen that replaces the elastic fibers of the tunica, and it may later calcify. The erectile tissue beneath is usually normal at first, which is why curvature, not loss of erection, is the presenting problem.

Because the plaque cannot stretch, the erect penis bends toward it. Most plaques are dorsal, giving an upward curve. There is often an early active phase, lasting roughly a year or more, with pain on erection and changing curvature, followed by a stable phase in which pain usually resolves but the deformity and a palpable plaque remain. Other effects are shortening, an indentation or hourglass narrowing, and erectile dysfunction when fibrosis disrupts the veno-occlusive mechanism or prevents rigidity beyond the plaque.

Middle age; palpable plaque; curvature toward plaque; painful erection early
Uneven development of the corpora, no plaque
Present since puberty; painless; no palpable lesion
Acute tear of the tunica albuginea during erection
History of prolonged erection; erectile dysfunction, no focal plaque
blocks.caption: Peyronie disease is the only one of these with a focal acquired plaque in the tunica.

sections.title: Male infertility: pretesticular, testicular, and post-testicular

blocks.text: Infertility is failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse, and a male factor contributes in about half of couples. Spermatogenesis needs pulsatile GnRH, LH acting on Leydig cells to make testosterone, very high intratesticular testosterone, FSH acting on Sertoli cells, a testis kept below core temperature, and open ducts. Sertoli cells secrete inhibin B, which feeds back on FSH. Locating the defect before, within, or after the testis therefore predicts the hormone pattern.

blocks.title: Male infertility by level
rows: Low (serum androgen high with anabolic steroids)
Kallmann syndrome, pituitary disease, hyperprolactinemia, anabolic steroids
Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, varicocele, mumps orchitis, chemotherapy or radiation
Obstruction after epididymitis, vasectomy, CBAVD in cystic fibrosis, ejaculatory duct obstruction
blocks.caption: Hormones locate the lesion: low gonadotropins mean the signal is missing, high FSH means the tubules are failing, and normal values with azoospermia mean a blockage.

blocks.text: Pretesticular causes are hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. In Kallmann syndrome, GnRH neurons fail to migrate from the olfactory placode, so anosmia accompanies hypogonadism. Prolactinomas suppress GnRH pulses. Anabolic steroids suppress GnRH, LH, and FSH by negative feedback; intratesticular testosterone falls and spermatogenesis stops even though serum androgen is high, and the testes shrink.

Testicular causes damage the tubules directly, so inhibin B falls and FSH rises. In Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) the tubules hyalinize, giving small firm testes, azoospermia, and high FSH and LH. In cryptorchidism, the higher temperature of the abdomen or inguinal canal injures germ cells, and bilateral cases cause the greatest loss. Varicocele works through heat and oxidative stress (C05). Mumps orchitis develops in a minority of men infected after puberty, is usually unilateral, and can leave tubular atrophy; sterility requires bilateral damage and is uncommon.

Post-testicular causes leave production and hormones normal but block delivery. In cystic fibrosis, CFTR mutations cause congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD) in nearly all affected men. The seminal vesicles, which supply most semen volume and its fructose, are often absent or hypoplastic, so the ejaculate is low in volume, acidic, fructose-poor, and free of sperm. Retrograde ejaculation (diabetic autonomic neuropathy, bladder neck surgery) also lowers volume, but sperm appear in post-ejaculatory urine. Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) sits outside this scheme: count is normal, but sperm are immotile from defective dynein arms.

blocks.title: Reading an infertility workup
blocks.text: A 28-year-old man has azoospermia. Case 1: semen volume 0.6 mL, acidic, no fructose; FSH, LH, and testosterone normal; testes normal size. Sperm are made but cannot leave and seminal vesicle fluid is missing, so the lesion is post-testicular: CBAVD, and CFTR testing follows. Case 2: volume normal; FSH and LH high, testosterone low, testes small and firm. The tubules have failed and inhibin B is low, so the lesion is testicular, and a karyotype showing 47,XXY confirms Klinefelter syndrome. Case 3: muscular build, FSH and LH very low, testes small. Exogenous androgen has switched off the axis, a pretesticular cause.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology explain most of the bedside findings. Descent of the testis behind the processus vaginalis accounts for hydrocele and indirect hernia, the shape of the tunica vaginalis accounts for torsion, the asymmetric venous drainage of the testes accounts for left varicocele and its link to renal cell carcinoma, and the countercurrent arrangement of the pampiniform plexus links varicocele and cryptorchidism to infertility through heat. Physics then completes the examination: clear fluid transmits light, while blood, veins, and tissue do not.

Physiology and pathology explain the penile disorders as failures of one hemodynamic system. Erection requires NO and cGMP to relax smooth muscle and the tunica albuginea to occlude venous outflow, so ED reflects damage to nerves, endothelium, arteries, or hormones; ischemic priapism is outflow that will not reopen; and Peyronie disease is a tunica that will not stretch. Fibrosis is the common end point of ischemic priapism and Peyronie disease, and both can cause ED. These categories overlap in real patients, and the classic signs (an absent cremasteric reflex, transillumination) are useful but imperfect, which is why imaging confirms what the examination suggests.

summary: Erection follows parasympathetic S2 to S4 release of NO, cGMP-mediated smooth muscle relaxation, sinusoidal filling, and compression of subtunical venules against the tunica albuginea.
ED is vascular, neurogenic, endocrine, drug-induced, or psychogenic; preserved nocturnal and morning erections show intact peripheral machinery and point to a psychogenic cause.
Hydrocele (clear fluid around the testis) and spermatocele (sperm-filled epididymal cyst separate from the testis) transilluminate; hematocele and varicocele, which contain blood, do not.

A patent processus vaginalis gives a communicating hydrocele that changes size with posture; noncommunicating hydroceles follow fluid imbalance from infection, trauma, tumor, or lymphatic obstruction.
A spermatocele and a simple epididymal cyst look the same; only sperm in the fluid separates them, and both are benign.
Varicocele is a refluxing pampiniform plexus, usually left-sided because the left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein; it impairs spermatogenesis mainly by heat.
A new left varicocele in an older man, or a right or nondecompressing one, suggests venous obstruction such as renal cell carcinoma in the renal vein or a retroperitoneal mass.

Torsion in a bell-clapper testis blocks veins before arteries, causing hemorrhagic infarction; sudden pain, a high-riding testis, and an absent cremasteric reflex are the clues, and viability falls after about 6 hours.
Ischemic priapism is painful, hypoxic, and acidotic (sickle cell disease, alpha-1 blocking drugs) and ends in fibrosis and ED; nonischemic priapism follows trauma and is painless with arterial blood.

Peyronie disease is a fibrous tunica albuginea plaque that bends the erect penis toward it; infertility is pretesticular (low gonadotropins), testicular (high FSH), or post-testicular (normal hormones, obstruction).

verify: Prevalence figures for varicocele (about 15% of men, about 90% left-sided) and the share of infertile men with varicocele vary between sources; confirm the values NABNE expects.
The timing of testicular viability after torsion (most salvageable within about 6 hours, few after about 24 hours) differs slightly among series.
The frequency with which the bell-clapper deformity is bilateral is reported differently in different studies; this chapter says only that it is often bilateral.

Sources differ on the afferent limb of the cremasteric reflex (ilioinguinal nerve, femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve, or both); the efferent limb is the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.

Cavernosal blood gas thresholds for ischemic priapism (pO2 below about 30 mmHg, pCO2 above about 60 mmHg, pH below about 7.25) and the 12, 24, and 48 hour stages of tissue injury come from urologic consensus statements rather than the core texts.
The interval by which vascular ED precedes symptomatic coronary disease is quoted from about 2 to 5 years; this chapter says only a few years.
Rates of mumps orchitis after puberty and of bilateral involvement vary widely by series; confirm whether NABNE tests specific percentages.
Semen analysis reference limits were revised in the WHO laboratory manual (2021 edition); confirm which edition NABNE uses before stating numerical cutoffs, which are omitted here.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Leriche syndrome, Kallmann syndrome, and Kartagener syndrome or only the descriptive terms.
Requested new diagram name for a future revision: scrotal-masses (testis, epididymis, tunica vaginalis, and cord showing the sites of hydrocele, hematocele, spermatocele, and varicocele).
